grade.why: X mirrors the reference with two null-coalescing reassignments. Y gets the same behaviour but rewrites the signature, adds an early return and uses optional chaining, which is more change than the task needed.

Both candidates are byte-identical one-line regex changes that add a negative lookahead for `gap`, `row-gap` and `column-gap`, so these keys get `px` like in the reference while other grid properties are unaffected.
Both patches have the same logic; Y's `Response | undefined` declaration matches the reference and repo idiom, while X's `Response | void = undefined` is slightly awkward.
Both skip undefined values and return NaN for empty or all-undefined input, but Y reuses the existing compat `sumBy` helper as the reference does, while X reimplements its summing loop inline.

The two candidates are byte-identical: both match the reference's nested-path and nullish fix, and both also move the function-criterion check ahead of the null check, so functions run on nullish elements as in lodash.

Both delegate non-function, non-array shorthands to the compat `iteratee`, which matches the reference behaviour; Y's imported `iteratee` is shadowed by the local `const iteratee` in `intersectionBy`, which is confusing, whereas X aliases the import as `createIteratee` like the reference does.

Both apply the same isIterateeCall gating as the reference, but Y also moves the toString call after the guard check, which matches lodash's order yet was not needed for the task, while X makes only the necessary change.

Both delegate to the shared `iteratee` utility and pass only the element to the callback, but X inlines this cleanly while Y keeps a helper that needs an awkward `Parameters<typeof iteratee>[0]` cast.
X matches the reference and lodash's `props || []` semantics exactly. Y's `??` leaves other falsy inputs such as `false` or `0` unhandled, and may change output in the exact-size bundle-size test.

Both lowercase the retainedHeaders list, which fixes the mixed-case match; X stops there, while Y also rewrites how the 304 response is built (copying res.headers and then setting ETag), a change the task did not need that adds regression risk.
Both candidates are identical to the reference patch, using Array.prototype.reverse.call to support array-like objects.

Y returns the short-circuit Response from some() exactly as the reference does, while X only assigns c.res as a side effect and still returns undefined, which breaks callers or tests that expect the returned value.

Both candidates make the same logical change: they match the reference fix and also call function criteria on nullish elements, which is arguably closer to lodash but goes beyond what the task needed; the only difference is the loop variable name (`index` vs `i`).
X reuses the existing compat sumBy exactly like the reference with a one-line change, while Y hand-rolls the same undefined-skipping sum loop that sumBy already provides.

Both candidates are functionally identical to the reference, adding a new three-key helper and returning early in updateWith, and they differ only in the helper's name and its location under compat/_internal.
Both candidates are identical to the reference patch: they use the existing isArrayLike helper and Array.from so `length` is no longer included as a sortable value.

X matches the reference exactly with a concise `Array.from(collection)`; Y is functionally equivalent (it even indexes strings by code unit, as lodash does) but adds a more verbose index-mapping construction.
Both candidates are identical to the reference patch, using Array.prototype.reverse.call to support array-like objects.

Both lowercase the configured header names, which fixes the bug, but X also rewrites how the 304 response is built; that change was not needed and risks altering behaviour, while Y is the minimal fix.

Both make the same behavioural change as the reference. Y does it with a local helper and adds no new file, so it is more minimal. X adds a separate internal module, which is closer to the reference's structure but goes beyond what the task needed.

X adds a narrow `(?!.*gap$)` lookahead that matches the reference's behaviour, while Y rewrites the grid branch to list only row/column, which also starts adding px to numeric grid-template-* values beyond the task's scope.

X matches the reference exactly, while Y also passes the tests and runs the guard check on the raw string before `toString` (as lodash does), so non-string array elements are handled correctly, at the cost of a small extra reorder.
